```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Liu_2024_cetirizine"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Liu_2024_cetirizine"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2024.1322788> (open access; the
  parameter table is Supplementary Table S1)
* Structural source: Pitsiu et al. 2004,
  <https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-2125.2003.02017.x> (free full text in PubMed
  Central, PMC1884474)

Liu 2024 did not build a new structural model. Its sparse real-world data (up to
three samples per child, few in the absorption phase) were used to re-fit the
Pitsiu 2004 paediatric cetirizine model. After an external evaluation showed
misspecification across the exposure range, the age slope on CL/F, the V/F
intercept, the IIV on CL/F and V/F and the proportional residual error were
re-estimated. All absorption parameters, both sex-specific CL/F intercepts and
the V/F age slope stayed fixed at the Pitsiu 2004 values. Liu 2024 describes the
covariate relationships in prose only. The equations below are the ones printed
in Pitsiu 2004 Table 4, and the parameter names in Liu's Supplementary Table S1
(`CL_AGE`, `CL_SEX on Male`, `CL_SEX on Female`, `V`, `V_AGE`, `Ka`) map onto
them one to one:

* CL/F (L/h) = `CL_AGE` x AGE + `CL_SEX,M` x (1 - SEXF) + `CL_SEX,F` x SEXF
* V/F (L) = `V` + `V_AGE` x AGE
* ka (1/h) = theta_ka + CL/V

# Population

Liu 2024 ran a prospective cohort study at Peking University Third Hospital
(April 2020 to April 2021) in 63 Chinese children with allergic diseases (38
male, 25 female). They were aged 6.34 +/- 3.7 years, weighed 26.4 +/- 15.7 kg
and were 120.1 +/- 27.7 cm tall (Results 3.1). Thirty-nine children received
label doses and 24 received off-label doses of up to twice the label dose
(Table 1); five of those exceeded 0.25 mg/kg per administration (Table 3).
Children with abnormal liver or kidney function were excluded. Each child gave
up to three plasma samples, measured by HPLC-MS/MS.

The same information is available programmatically:

```{r population}
str(readModelDb("Liu_2024_cetirizine")()$population)
```

# Source trace

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| `lcl` (CL/F intercept, male) | `fixed(log(0.771))` L/h | Liu 2024 Table S1 'CL_SEX on Male' 0.771 FIXED; Pitsiu 2004 Table 4 |
| `lcl_female` (CL/F intercept, female) | `fixed(log(0.592))` L/h | Liu 2024 Table S1 'CL_SEX on Female' 0.592 FIXED; Pitsiu 2004 Table 4 |
| `e_age_cl` | 0.28 L/h/year | Liu 2024 Table S1 'CL_AGE' (RSE 17%); Discussion 4.1 '0.28 in our results' |
| `lvc` (V/F intercept) | `log(23.1)` L | Liu 2024 Table S1 'V' (RSE 40%) |
| `e_age_vc` | `fixed(1.42)` L/year | Liu 2024 Table S1 'V_AGE' 1.42 FIXED; Pitsiu 2004 Table 4 |
| `lka` (theta_ka) | `fixed(log(2.14))` 1/h | Liu 2024 Table S1 'Ka' 2.14 FIXED; Pitsiu 2004 Table 4 |
| `etalcl` | 0.378 | Liu 2024 Table S1 'IIV_CL/F' (RSE 34%, shrinkage 21.2%) |
| `etalvc` | 0.445 | Liu 2024 Table S1 'IIV_V/F' (RSE 41%, shrinkage 47.1%) |
| `etalka` | `fixed(2.1)` | Liu 2024 Table S1 'IIV_Ka' 2.1 FIXED (Pitsiu 2004: 145% CV, 1.45^2 = 2.10) |
| `propSd` | 0.36 | Liu 2024 Table S1 'Proportional error' (RSE 16%); 'Sigma' 1 FIXED |
| CL/F, V/F equations | n/a | Pitsiu 2004 Table 4; Liu 2024 Methods 2.4.2 (prose) |
| ka = theta_ka + CL/V | n/a | Pitsiu 2004 Table 4 footnote; Liu 2024 Methods 2.4.2 |
| One compartment, first-order absorption | n/a | Liu 2024 Methods 2.4.2 |
| `Cc = central / vc * 1000` (ng/mL) | n/a | Unit conversion: dose in mg, V/F in L |

# Typical CL/F and V/F by age: Liu 2024 vs Pitsiu 2004

Re-estimating the age slope on CL/F (0.12 to 0.28 L/h/year) and the V/F
intercept (4.00 to 23.1 L) gives Chinese children a higher clearance and a much
larger apparent volume than the Pitsiu 2004 European children of the same age.
The table sets the typical values of both models against each other, with the
Pitsiu values from Pitsiu 2004 Table 5.

```{r typical-by-age}
mod <- readModelDb("Liu_2024_cetirizine")
th <- rxode2::rxode(mod)$theta
ages <- c(0.5, 2, 6, 7, 12)
typical <- tibble(AGE = ages) |>
  mutate(
    liu_cl_m = th[["e_age_cl"]] * AGE + exp(th[["lcl"]]),
    liu_cl_f = th[["e_age_cl"]] * AGE + exp(th[["lcl_female"]]),
    liu_v = exp(th[["lvc"]]) + th[["e_age_vc"]] * AGE,
    pitsiu_cl_m = c(0.83, 1.01, 1.49, 1.61, 2.21),
    pitsiu_cl_f = c(0.65, 0.83, 1.31, 1.43, 2.03),
    pitsiu_v = c(4.71, 6.84, 12.5, 13.9, 21.0)
  )
typical |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Age (years)" = AGE,
    "Liu CL/F male (L/h)" = liu_cl_m,
    "Liu CL/F female (L/h)" = liu_cl_f,
    "Liu V/F (L)" = liu_v,
    "Pitsiu CL/F male (L/h)" = pitsiu_cl_m,
    "Pitsiu CL/F female (L/h)" = pitsiu_cl_f,
    "Pitsiu V/F (L)" = pitsiu_v
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Typical apparent clearance and volume by age.")
```

The model reproduces Pitsiu's Table 5 exactly when Pitsiu's own estimates
(0.12 L/h/year and 4.00 L) replace Liu's. That confirms the equations encoded
here are the ones Pitsiu printed:

```{r pitsiu-equation-check}
pitsiu_check <- typical |>
  mutate(
    cl_m = 0.12 * AGE + exp(th[["lcl"]]),
    cl_f = 0.12 * AGE + exp(th[["lcl_female"]]),
    v = 4.00 + th[["e_age_vc"]] * AGE
  )
# Pitsiu Table 5 is printed to 2-3 significant figures.
stopifnot(
  max(abs(pitsiu_check$cl_m - pitsiu_check$pitsiu_cl_m)) < 0.011,
  max(abs(pitsiu_check$cl_f - pitsiu_check$pitsiu_cl_f)) < 0.011,
  max(abs(pitsiu_check$v - pitsiu_check$pitsiu_v)) < 0.06
)
```

# Virtual cohort: the twelve label-dose patients of Table 2

Liu 2024 Table 2 lists twelve virtual girls aged 1 to 12 years, each at the
maximum label dose, and reports the median steady-state Cmax and Cmin over
1,000 simulations. Body weight and height are listed in that table but are not
model covariates. Each patient is simulated here with 200 subjects (the
package's per-arm cap), dosed for 30 days. The last 24 hours, 696 to 720 h, are
the steady-state window; Figure 1 of the paper covers the same window.

```{r cohort}
table2 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~pid, ~regimen, ~amt, ~ii, ~AGE, ~SEXF, ~cmax_pub, ~cmin_pub,
  1, "2.5 mg bid", 2.5, 12, 1, 1, 232.27, 156.48,
  2, "5 mg qd", 5, 24, 2, 1, 243.06, 86.27,
  3, "5 mg qd", 5, 24, 3, 1, 225.75, 71.94,
  4, "5 mg qd", 5, 24, 4, 1, 204.98, 47.53,
  5, "5 mg qd", 5, 24, 5, 1, 186.70, 48.09,
  6, "5 mg qd", 5, 24, 6, 1, 160.15, 31.70,
  7, "10 mg qd", 10, 24, 7, 1, 306.93, 55.57,
  8, "10 mg qd", 10, 24, 8, 1, 270.42, 38.28,
  9, "10 mg qd", 10, 24, 9, 1, 259.97, 32.19,
  10, "10 mg qd", 10, 24, 10, 1, 227.78, 37.98,
  11, "10 mg qd", 10, 24, 11, 1, 234.20, 28.80,
  12, "10 mg qd", 10, 24, 12, 1, 209.28, 18.94
) |>
  mutate(patient = sprintf("Age %d y, %s", AGE, regimen))

n_per_patient <- 200
t_end <- 720
t_ss <- t_end - 24

make_patient <- function(row, id_offset) {
  ids <- id_offset + seq_len(n_per_patient)
  dose_times <- seq(0, t_end - row$ii, by = row$ii)
  obs_times <- seq(t_ss - 16, t_end, by = 0.25)
  doses <- tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = dose_times) |>
    mutate(amt = row$amt, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot")
  obs <- tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = obs_times) |>
    mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central")
  bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    mutate(AGE = row$AGE, SEXF = row$SEXF, patient = row$patient)
}

events <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(table2)), function(i) {
  make_patient(table2[i, ], id_offset = (i - 1L) * n_per_patient)
})) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unique(events[, c("id", "time", "evid")])))
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20240314)
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, keep = c("patient")) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

# Replicate Figure 1

Figure 1 of Liu 2024 plots one curve per age over the steady-state window. The
paper does not say whether that curve is the typical value or the median of the
simulations. The median curve is plotted here, on the paper's hourly grid.

```{r figure-1, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
median_curve <- sim |>
  filter(abs(time - round(time)) < 1e-9) |>
  group_by(patient, time) |>
  summarise(Cc = median(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(table2 |> select(patient, AGE), by = "patient")

ggplot(median_curve, aes(time, Cc, colour = factor(AGE), group = patient)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(680, 705), ylim = c(0, 400)) +
  labs(
    x = "Time after first dose (h)", y = "Cetirizine concentration (ng/mL)",
    colour = "Age (years)",
    title = "Figure 1: steady state at the label dose, ages 1-12 years",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 1 of Liu 2024 (median of 200 simulated subjects per age)."
  )
```

# PKNCA validation against Table 2

PKNCA computes Cmax and Cmin per subject over the steady-state window. The
median across the 200 subjects of each patient is compared with Table 2.

```{r pknca}
sim_nca <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc), time >= t_ss) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, patient)

dose_df <- events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1, time >= t_ss) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, patient)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | patient + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | patient + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = t_ss, end = t_end, cmax = TRUE, cmin = TRUE, tmax = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

published <- table2 |>
  select(patient, cmax = cmax_pub, cmin = cmin_pub)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_res,
  reference = published,
  by = "patient",
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", cmin = "ng/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = "Median simulated vs. published (Table 2) steady-state Cmax and Cmin. * differs from reference by >20%."
)
```

The simulated troughs scatter on both sides of Table 2. Most are within about
25%; the misses run both high and low, which looks like Monte-Carlo noise in a
200-subject median of a highly variable trough rather than a bias. The
per-subject median Cmax is consistently above Table 2, by roughly 5-30%. That is what you would
expect if the paper read Cmax off the median concentration-time curve on an
hourly grid (the curve of its Figure 1), not as the median of per-subject
maxima: with an absorption rate constant as variable as this one (fixed IIV
variance 2.1), subjects peak at different times, so the median of the
individual peaks sits above the peak of the median curve. The same metric taken
from the median curve agrees more closely:

```{r median-curve-metric}
curve_metric <- median_curve |>
  filter(time >= t_ss) |>
  group_by(patient) |>
  summarise(cmax_sim = max(Cc), cmin_sim = min(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(table2 |> select(pid, patient, cmax_pub, cmin_pub), by = "patient") |>
  arrange(pid) |>
  mutate(
    cmax_pct = 100 * (cmax_sim / cmax_pub - 1),
    cmin_pct = 100 * (cmin_sim / cmin_pub - 1)
  )

curve_metric |>
  select(patient, cmax_sim, cmax_pub, cmax_pct, cmin_sim, cmin_pub, cmin_pct) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Patient" = patient,
    "Cmax,ss sim (ng/mL)" = cmax_sim,
    "Cmax,ss Table 2" = cmax_pub,
    "Cmax diff (%)" = cmax_pct,
    "Cmin,ss sim (ng/mL)" = cmin_sim,
    "Cmin,ss Table 2" = cmin_pub,
    "Cmin diff (%)" = cmin_pct
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Peak and trough of the median curve (hourly grid) vs. Table 2.")

# Structural check on the centre of the twelve patients. A mis-transcribed
# clearance slope (0.12 vs 0.28 L/h/year) or volume intercept (4.0 vs 23.1 L)
# moves these medians by far more than 25%; the per-patient values carry the
# Monte-Carlo noise of 200 subjects and the unknown details of the paper's
# summary, so no per-patient bound is asserted. Across draws the medians
# were about +4% to +9% (Cmax) and +8% to +19% (Cmin); the trough of a
# 200-subject cohort is the noisier of the two, hence its wider bound.
stopifnot(
  abs(median(curve_metric$cmax_pct)) < 20,
  abs(median(curve_metric$cmin_pct)) < 35
)
```

For ages 3 to 12 the median-curve peak is within about 15% of Table 2. The
youngest patients (1 year on 2.5 mg bid and 2 years on 5 mg qd) come out about
10-25% higher than Table 2; the source does not report enough about its
simulation to explain the difference.

The paper's main finding is reproduced by the typical-value (no IIV) curves.
Among the label doses the 7-year-old has the highest steady-state peak (the
first age at 10 mg qd) and the 6-year-old the lowest (the oldest age at 5 mg
qd), because the label dose steps up with age while CL/F and V/F rise
continuously:

```{r typical-ordering}
sim_tv <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  rxode2::zeroRe(mod),
  events = events |> filter(id %% n_per_patient == 1),
  keep = c("patient")
) |>
  as.data.frame()

tv_peaks <- sim_tv |>
  filter(time >= t_ss) |>
  group_by(patient) |>
  summarise(cmax_typical = max(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(table2 |> select(pid, patient, AGE), by = "patient") |>
  arrange(pid)
knitr::kable(
  tv_peaks |> select(patient, cmax_typical) |>
    dplyr::rename("Patient" = patient, "Typical Cmax,ss (ng/mL)" = cmax_typical),
  digits = 1
)

# Typical-value solve: no random draws, so the ordering is deterministic.
stopifnot(
  tv_peaks$AGE[which.max(tv_peaks$cmax_typical)] == 7,
  tv_peaks$AGE[which.min(tv_peaks$cmax_typical)] == 6
)
```

# Off-label and overdose scenarios

## Table 3 patients (doses above 0.25 mg/kg)

Liu 2024 Table 3 reports Bayesian (POSTHOC) simulations of five children who
received more than 0.25 mg/kg per dose. Those values use each child's
individual random effects, which are not published. The population-level
prediction for the same age, sex and regimen is shown for context only and is
not expected to match.

```{r table-3}
table3 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~patient_id, ~amt, ~AGE, ~SEXF, ~cmax_pub, ~cmin_pub,
  "6", 6.43, 4.08, 0, 417.67, 237.31,
  "45", 5, 6, 1, 236.64, 100.48,
  "54", 5, 5.7, 0, 266.31, 135.87,
  "58", 5, 5, 0, 277.34, 150.08,
  "66", 9, 4, 0, 580.68, 325.40
)

ev_t3 <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(table3)), function(i) {
  r <- table3[i, ]
  ids <- (i - 1L) * n_per_patient + seq_len(n_per_patient)
  bind_rows(
    tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = seq(0, 216 - 12, by = 12)) |>
      mutate(amt = r$amt, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot"),
    tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = seq(192, 216, by = 1)) |>
      mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central")
  ) |>
    mutate(AGE = r$AGE, SEXF = r$SEXF, patient_id = r$patient_id)
})) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))

sim_t3 <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = ev_t3, keep = c("patient_id")) |>
  as.data.frame()

sim_t3 |>
  filter(time >= 204) |>
  group_by(patient_id, time) |>
  summarise(Cc = median(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  summarise(cmax_sim = max(Cc), cmin_sim = min(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(table3, by = "patient_id") |>
  arrange(as.integer(patient_id)) |>
  select(patient_id, amt, AGE, cmax_sim, cmax_pub, cmin_sim, cmin_pub) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Patient" = patient_id,
    "Dose bid (mg)" = amt,
    "Age (years)" = AGE,
    "Cmax,ss population (ng/mL)" = cmax_sim,
    "Cmax,ss Table 3 POSTHOC" = cmax_pub,
    "Cmin,ss population (ng/mL)" = cmin_sim,
    "Cmin,ss Table 3 POSTHOC" = cmin_pub
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Population predictions for the Table 3 regimens (context only).")
```

## Figure 3: the 30 mg medication error

A 5-year-old boy prescribed 5 mg bid was given a single 30 mg dose 12 h after
his first 5 mg dose. A sample taken 2.5 h after the error measured
1725 ng/mL. Dosing restarted later. The curve in Figure 3 of the paper doses
again at about 48 and 72 h, which is the schedule simulated here. Figure 3 is
the boy's individual POSTHOC curve, which needs his unpublished random effects.
The population prediction interval below is shown with the measured
concentration for orientation.

```{r figure-3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
ids_od <- seq_len(n_per_patient)
ev_od <- bind_rows(
  tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids_od, tibble(time = c(0, 12, 48, 72), amt = c(5, 30, 5, 5))) |>
    mutate(evid = 1L, cmt = "depot"),
  tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids_od, time = seq(0, 80, by = 0.5)) |>
    mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central")
) |>
  mutate(AGE = 5, SEXF = 0) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))

sim_od <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = ev_od) |> as.data.frame()

od_summary <- sim_od |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(
    Q05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05), Q50 = median(Cc), Q95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(od_summary, aes(time, Q50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(time = 14.5, Q50 = 1725), colour = "black", size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Time after first dose (h)", y = "Cetirizine concentration (ng/mL)",
    title = "Figure 3: 30 mg medication error in a 5-year-old boy",
    caption = paste(
      "Population median and 90% interval (200 subjects). Point: measured",
      "1725 ng/mL, 2.5 h after the 30 mg dose. Replicates the setting of Figure 3 of Liu 2024."
    )
  )

od_summary |>
  filter(time == 14.5) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Time (h)" = time, "5th percentile" = Q05, "Median" = Q50, "95th percentile" = Q95
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Population prediction 2.5 h after the 30 mg dose (ng/mL).")
```

The measured 1725 ng/mL lies well above the population median, in the upper
tail of the interval. The paper's individual fit, which uses the boy's own
random effects, passes a peak of about 1,780 ng/mL through it.

# Assumptions and deviations

- **Equations from Pitsiu 2004.** Liu 2024 names the covariate effects
  (`CL_AGE`, `CL_SEX`, `V`, `V_AGE`) but does not print the equations. They were
  taken from Pitsiu 2004 Table 4, the model Liu re-fitted. The Pitsiu
  typical-value check above reproduces Pitsiu's Table 5 from those equations.
- **Concentration units.** Liu 2024 Tables 2 and 3 and the Results text label
  concentrations as ug/mL, but the axes of Figures 1-3 read ng/mL, Pitsiu 2004
  modelled ng/mL from doses in ug, and 10 mg into a V/F of about 30 L can only
  give hundreds of ng/mL. The model reports ng/mL, and the ug/mL labels in the
  paper are treated as a typographical error.
- **IIV values are variances.** Liu's Table S1 IIV column is read as the
  NONMEM OMEGA variance. The fixed ka entry, 2.1, is exactly the square of the
  145% CV Pitsiu reported (1.45^2 = 2.10), which identifies the scale.
- **Residual error.** Table S1 lists a 'Proportional error' of 0.36 alongside
  'Sigma 1 FIXED'. This is the THETA-scaled residual form, so 0.36 is the
  proportional SD.
- **No bioavailability term.** CL/F and V/F are apparent parameters and the
  oral dose enters the depot with F = 1, as in Pitsiu 2004.
- **Sex coding.** Pitsiu coded SEX = 1 for female, which is the canonical
  `SEXF` directly.
- **Cohort size.** Table 2 summarises 1,000 simulations per patient. This
  vignette uses 200 per patient, so the per-patient medians carry more
  Monte-Carlo noise than the paper's.
- **Steady-state window.** The paper does not state how long it dosed before
  reading steady state. Figure 1's axis (680-705 h) and the doses at 684 and
  696 h suggest about 30 days, which is what is simulated here.
- **Cohort size reported inconsistently.** The modelling text gives 63
  children, but Table 1 adds up to 65 across age groups and the safety section
  refers to 66 patients. The population metadata uses 63.
- No correction notice for Liu 2024 or Pitsiu 2004 was found in Europe PMC
  as of 2026-10-29.
